questions.q: Why are silent bugs considered more dangerous in research code than loud bugs?
options: Silent bugs are always harder to write code for
Loud bugs crash and force a fix before the job can proceed, while silent bugs let the job run to completion and produce a plausible-looking but wrong result
Silent bugs only occur in production, never in research code
Loud bugs take longer to debug than silent bugs
questions.explain: A loud bug (exception, crash) is self-correcting because the job can't proceed until it's fixed. A silent bug has no such mechanism — it can produce a wrong number that gets reported before anyone notices.

questions.q: In the example where `preds` has shape (B,) and `targets` has shape (B, 1), what actually happens when computing `(preds - targets) ** 2`?
options: PyTorch raises a shape-mismatch error immediately
The operation broadcasts to shape (B, B) instead of performing the intended elementwise (B,) comparison, silently producing a wrong result
PyTorch automatically squeezes the extra dimension and computes the correct result
The operation returns a scalar zero
questions.explain: Broadcasting rules expand (B,) and (B,1) to (B,B), which is a completely different computation than the intended elementwise comparison. No error is raised, so the bug is silent.

questions.q: What is the practical risk of forgetting to call `model.train()` after an evaluation pass that used `model.eval()`?
options: The next training step will crash with a RuntimeError
Dropout and batch norm continue behaving as they do in eval mode for subsequent training steps, silently biasing results with no error raised
The optimizer will refuse to call .step()
Gradients will stop being computed entirely
questions.explain: Leaving the model in eval mode means dropout is disabled and batch norm uses running statistics instead of batch statistics — a silent behavioral change with no exception raised.

questions.q: What does omitting `optimizer.zero_grad()` between training steps cause?
options: An immediate crash with an out-of-memory error
Gradients from previous steps silently accumulate with the current step's gradients, inflating the effective step size without any error
The loss value becomes NaN on the very next step
PyTorch automatically zeroes gradients internally, so nothing happens
questions.explain: Without zeroing, gradients accumulate across calls to backward(), silently changing the effective update magnitude in a way that depends on how many steps were affected — no exception is raised.

questions.q: What does `torch.autograd.set_detect_anomaly(True)` do that helps convert a silent bug into a loud one?
options: It automatically fixes any NaN values found during training
It raises an exception at the exact operation in the backward pass that produced a NaN or Inf, instead of letting it propagate silently
It disables all gradient computation to save memory
It prevents the model from ever producing NaN values
questions.explain: Anomaly detection mode pinpoints exactly which backward operation produced a NaN/Inf and raises there, rather than letting the corrupted value silently propagate through the rest of the computation graph.
